opus-5.5.text:
I think it mattered because it was the first time I really understood that the tools I was using weren't magic. In high school, like a lot of students, I was writing small programs, doing some competition-style coding, and the compiler was just this black box: you type code in, something runs. When I decided to build a little transpiler, basically taking a simple language I made up and translating it into another language that could actually run, I had to confront every layer myself. How do you parse text into a structure? How do you represent the program internally? How do you walk that representation and generate something equivalent on the other side?

None of it was sophisticated. Looking back, the code was probably pretty messy. But the experience gave me a very concrete feeling for what an abstraction is, and that you can build your own abstractions instead of only consuming other people's. That mindset ended up shaping a lot of what I did later. When I worked on things like XGBoost, or later TVM and machine learning compilers, the core question was always similar: here is a high-level description of what you want to compute, how do you systematically transform it into something efficient on real hardware? In some sense it's the same pattern I first touched as a teenager, just at a much bigger scale.

There's also a more personal side. Building something end to end, where nobody gives you a template, teaches you a kind of confidence. You run into bugs you don't understand, you get stuck, and you slowly dig your way out. That process of "I don't know how this works yet, but I can figure it out by building it" is probably the most important habit I took from that project. I tell students now: don't be afraid to rebuild something that already exists, even a toy version. The point isn't to compete with the real thing. The point is that afterward, you see the whole stack differently, and you start noticing places where you could do something new.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think when I was in high school, I actually did some competitive programming, so I was exposed to writing programs that run correctly and run fast. But at some point I got really curious about what actually happens underneath. You write code in one language, and then somehow it becomes something the machine can run. That felt like magic to me, and I don't like things being magic.

So I decided to just try to build one. It was a very small thing, basically taking a subset of a language, parsing it, and emitting code in another, lower-level form. Nothing anybody would use. But the process of doing it changed how I looked at computing. Suddenly a compiler wasn't a black box anymore. I understood that every abstraction is layered on top of another abstraction, and you can go down one layer and change things if you want to.

I think that is really the key lesson, and it is one I kept coming back to. Later on, when we built XGBoost, and then TVM, and the whole machine learning compilation direction, the core question was always the same. There is a gap between what people want to express and what the hardware can efficiently run. And somebody has to build the bridge. The mini transpiler was my first time building that bridge, even if it was a tiny one.

The other thing it taught me is that you learn much more from building a full, end-to-end system than from reading about it. A lot of my understanding did not come from the textbook, it came from hitting a bug at two in the morning and realizing I misunderstood how scoping works. So when students ask me how to get into systems or ML systems, I always say, pick something that feels a bit too hard, and build it from scratch. You don't need to finish perfectly. The understanding you gain along the way is the real outcome.

I think it was important because it gave me the experience of taking an idea and making it work end to end. When you build a mini transpiler from scratch, you have to figure out how to represent a program, transform it, and produce something that actually runs. Even with a small project, those pieces have to fit together.

For me, the value was less about how sophisticated the result was and more about the confidence that came from building it. Something that initially seemed complicated became a series of problems I could work through. That made me more willing to explore unfamiliar ideas and learn by implementing them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it was important because it gave me the confidence to build something I didn’t fully understand at the beginning. A transpiler sounds complicated, but once you break it down—reading the input, understanding its structure, and generating code—you can make progress step by step. Building a small version from scratch helped me see how those pieces fit together.

The lasting lesson was that I could learn by building. You don’t have to understand an entire field before you start experimenting with it. Sometimes making a small, working system is what helps you understand the bigger ideas.
